prompt: Write a first-person detective story featuring a locked-room murder case. The story should be tightly plotted with strong suspense.

outline.name: The Telegram
outline.description: Victor Hale, a disgraced former homicide detective now scraping by on insurance fraud cases, receives an urgent telegram from Arthur Pemberton: 'He is alive. Come to Blackwood Peak. If I am found dead, the answer is in the wall.' Victor had once dismissed Arthur's paranoid letters as ramblings, but the enclosed bank draft is enough to make him accept. He takes the funicular up to the isolated Blackwood Peak Hotel, a converted Victorian mansion stranded on a glacier, just as a blizzard buries the tracks behind him. At dinner he meets the other stranded guests: Marcus Webb, Arthur's resentful business partner; Celia Pemberton, Arthur's estranged actress wife; Ruth Keene, his devoted secretary; and Elias, a strange night porter. Arthur never appears. That night, Victor is woken by a scream from the east wing.

outline.name: The Locked Door
outline.description: Victor breaks into Arthur's suite with Sheriff Calder, his old rival from the city force. The heavy oak door is bolted from the inside with a solid brass bolt. The windows are frosted shut, sealed by a century of paint. The chimney is too narrow for even a child. Arthur Pemberton lies dead near the fireplace, two deep stab wounds in his chest and a defensive gash across his forearm. Calder declares it suicide, mocking Victor's ruined career. Victor points out that no man stabs himself twice and then slashes his own arm in self-defense. He takes charge of the scene, searching for a weapon that is nowhere to be found. The room is sealed, the body is murdered, and the killer has vanished into thin air.

outline.name: The Suspects
outline.description: Victor and Calder interview the trapped guests. Marcus Webb claims he was drinking alone in the lounge, but no one can confirm it. Celia says she was in her room with a headache, yet her story is shaky and her hands are cold. Ruth Keene was supposedly typing, but she is evasive and keeps clutching her purse. Elias, the porter, swears that just before the scream he saw a dark shadow pass under Arthur's door—and then heard Arthur cry out, 'You're dead!' Each suspect has a motive: Marcus faced financial ruin, Celia was about to be cut off, Ruth's position depended on Arthur's will, and Elias seems to know more than he admits. Calder insists the locked room makes suicide the only possible answer, but Victor refuses to accept it. The blizzard has cut them off from the world; the killer is still among them.

outline.name: The Letter
outline.description: Victor returns to the suite alone, hoping to find something the others missed. In the inner pocket of Arthur's coat, he finds a letter addressed to him, written hours before the murder. Arthur repeats his warning: his twin brother, Silas, presumed dead in a boating accident twenty years ago, is alive and hiding in the hotel. 'He knows the old ways of this house. If I am found dead, the answer is in the wall.' Victor is flooded with guilt—he had dismissed the earlier letters as paranoid rambling. He re-tests the locked room: bolt, windows, chimney. No exit. Yet the letter insists. He begins tapping the walls and discovers a seam in the wainscoting. He pries it open and finds a narrow dark opening.

outline.name: The Priest-Hole
outline.description: Victor opens the hidden panel and finds a priest-hole: a narrow vertical compartment just wide enough for a man. The dust has been recently disturbed. There are fresh footprints, a dropped cufflink, and a faint smell of tobacco. But the back wall appears to be solid brick, and Victor concludes the killer could not have hidden there—there is no exit. He pockets the cufflink and dismisses the space as a dead end. Ruth Keene interrupts him, claiming she was looking for Arthur's will. She grows uneasy when she sees the open panel. After she leaves, Victor stares at the priest-hole and realizes the line of the brick is too regular to be natural. Before he can investigate further, another scream echoes through the corridor.

outline.name: The Shadow Under the Door
outline.description: The second scream turns out to be Celia, startled by a rat—or so she says. Victor is not convinced. He returns to Elias and forces him to repeat his account. Before the murder, a shadow slid across the band of light beneath Arthur's door, and then Arthur cried out. Victor reconstructs the scene: the door was bolted from inside, the room was lit, and the shadow came from someone moving inside the room. If Arthur had been alone, he could have made the shadow himself—but Elias heard Arthur scream at someone. That means a second person was inside the sealed room when the bolt was thrown. Victor realizes the killer must have been hiding in the room before Arthur locked himself in. The only hiding place is the priest-hole. He rushes back to the suite, determined to find the secret he missed.

outline.name: The Forged Signature
outline.description: Before Victor can reach the priest-hole, he catches Ruth Keene in Arthur's study, burning a document. He rescues it from the fire: a power-of-attorney transferring all of Arthur's assets to Ruth. The signature is a clumsy tracing from an old contract. Ruth breaks down and confesses she forged it, but swears she was trying to protect Arthur from Marcus Webb, who had been stealing from the company. She admits she saw Marcus enter Arthur's room earlier that night. Marcus denies it, and Celia retaliates by revealing that Ruth and Marcus were once lovers. The motives are multiplying, but the locked room still makes no sense. As Ruth leaves, Victor notices a smear of grease on her sleeve—the same grease from the priest-hole floor. He realizes she has been inside the hidden compartment too. He rushes back to the suite.

outline.name: The Boiler Room
outline.description: Victor returns to the priest-hole and, with a penknife, finds the spring catch in the false brick panel. The back of the compartment swings open, revealing a narrow service passage that winds down through the walls of the hotel. Victor follows it to an iron door that opens into the boiler room. There, hidden in an alcove, he finds a wet coat, a knife wrapped in oilcloth, and a faded photograph of two identical boys. Footsteps echo behind him. Silas Pemberton steps out of the shadows—gaunt, bearded, very much alive. He tells Victor he has been living in the forgotten passages of the hotel for days. Before Victor can draw his gun, Silas strikes him down. Victor collapses onto the concrete floor, the truth burning in his mind.

outline.name: The Twin
outline.description: Victor wakes tied to a pipe in the boiler room. Silas is feeding the murder weapon into the furnace. He speaks calmly, revealing everything: twenty years ago, he survived the boating accident, but Arthur left him to drown in order to claim the family inheritance. Silas has been hiding ever since, waiting for his chance. He entered Arthur's suite through the priest-hole before Arthur threw the bolt, killed him, and escaped through the hidden passage—creating a perfect locked room. The shadow Elias saw under the door was Silas crossing the room before the murder. Victor keeps Silas talking, appealing to the brother Arthur feared, until Sheriff Calder, following Victor's earlier note, bursts in with Elias. They overpower Silas and drag him into the light. Calder admits he was wrong. The locked room was never sealed—the killer had already been inside.

outline.name: Redemption
outline.description: The blizzard breaks, and the funicular is repaired. Silas is taken away, and the hidden passage is exposed to the authorities. Victor stands in the cold morning light, looking at the room that almost defeated him. He realizes the locked room was not a puzzle of bolts and walls, but a prison of his own perception. He had insisted the room was sealed because he could not accept that his judgment might be wrong—the same arrogance that had destroyed his career and cost an innocent man his freedom. He writes a letter of apology to Arthur's memory, and a second letter to the court, reopening the old wrongful conviction. The key to the locked room was never a key at all. It was a man who had already been inside—and the door Victor had to open was the one to his own closed mind.

chapters.name: The Telegram
chapters.content:
The telegram arrived on a Tuesday, folded around a bank draft for two hundred pounds, which is the only reason I read it twice.

I was Victor Hale, late of the city police—a homicide detective who had once been good enough to make the papers, and then foolish enough to make them twice. The second time cost me my badge, my pension, and any hope of entering a station house without someone remembering my name in that tone. These days I earned my bread chasing insurance fraud: husbands who drowned their boats, wives who burned their own kitchens. Work that paid poorly and asked no questions about my pride.

The telegram was from Arthur Pemberton. I had not thought of Arthur in years, and I had tried hard not to.

HE IS ALIVE. COME TO BLACKWOOD PEAK. IF I AM FOUND DEAD, THE ANSWER IS IN THE WALL.

I had seen Arthur's handwriting on half a dozen letters over the past year, each wilder than the last, each begging me to come north and believe him about the brother who had drowned. Silas, he wrote. Silas is not dead. Silas is coming back for what is his. I had read those letters over morning coffee and set them aside as the ravings of a rich man alone too long in a drafty house. Paranoid. Delusional. I had not answered a single one.

But two hundred pounds is a great persuader, and guilt is a better one. I wired my acceptance before I could think better of it, packed a bag, and took the night train north.

Blackwood Peak does not appear on most maps. It is a black fang of rock thrust up from the glacier fields, and on its shoulder, bolted to the stone like a bird's nest, sits the hotel Arthur's grandfather built—a Victorian mansion hauled up piece by piece a century ago, all turrets and gables, its windows staring out over the white emptiness as if daring it to come closer. The only way up is the funicular, a rusted iron cage that climbs the cliff on a single cable.

The funicular man was old enough to remember when the mountain had been a destination. He looked at the sky the way sailors look at a sea. "Storm's coming," he said. "Last car up tonight. You sure you want to be stranded up there?"

I told him I was expected. The cage shuddered and climbed, and below us the valley fell away until the world was only rock and snow and the thin scream of wind through the cable. Behind me the storm rolled in like a wall. By the time we reached the top, the tracks were already buried. The blizzard had closed the mountain like a fist.

The hotel swallowed me whole. Inside, it smelled of old wood and coal smoke and a century of trapped weather. A fire roared in the great hall, and around it the stranded guests had gathered like survivors of a shipwreck, which in a sense they were. There were four of them.

Marcus Webb shook my hand too hard and held it too long. Arthur's business partner, a bull of a man with a salesman's smile and eyes that kept drifting toward the bar. He had been drinking most of the afternoon, I judged, and he spoke of Arthur with the careful courtesy of a man who had spent years rehearsing his hatred.

Celia Pemberton did not rise when I entered. She sat in the deepest armchair with a glass of wine and the air of a woman once adored in theaters and now furious at every room that failed to applaud. Arthur's wife. Estranged, the letters had said, though estranged seemed a gentle word for the look that crossed her face at his name.

Ruth Keene was the only one who seemed genuinely worried. Small, precise, dressed in grey, with the ink-stained fingers of a woman who had spent twenty years at Arthur's side as his secretary. She had been crying, I thought, though she had washed her face carefully. She asked me, in a voice that trembled only slightly, whether I had heard from Mr. Pemberton, whether he had written, whether he was all right.

The fourth guest did not speak to me at all. He was the night porter, a man named Elias, who stood at the edge of the firelight the way shadows stand—present and yet apart. He had a gaunt, carved face and pale eyes, and when he spoke it was only to say that dinner would be served, and that Mr. Pemberton had asked to be excused.

Arthur never appeared.

We dined at a long table set for five, and the empty chair at its head grew heavier with every course. Marcus drank through the meal and grew loud about the company, about loans and ledgers and the ruin Arthur was steering them toward. Celia listened with a thin smile and said nothing. Ruth pushed her food around her plate and kept glancing at the door. And Elias stood against the wall, watching us all with those pale, patient eyes, as if waiting for something he already knew was coming.

When I asked where Arthur kept himself, there was a silence you could have hung a coat on.

"His suite," Ruth said at last. "The east wing. He's been in there for days. He says he's working."

"Working," Marcus repeated, and laughed without humor. "Or hiding. He's been hiding from something all winter. You've seen his letters, Hale. You know what he thinks."

I said nothing about the letters. But that night, alone in my room, with the wind screaming around the turrets and snow piling against the window, I took the telegram out and read it again by candlelight.

HE IS ALIVE. COME TO BLACKWOOD PEAK. IF I AM FOUND DEAD, THE ANSWER IS IN THE WALL.

Twenty years ago, Arthur's twin had gone overboard in a boating accident on the lake below this mountain. They found the boat, splintered against the rocks. They never found the body. And Arthur inherited everything—the fortune, the company, the hotel on the glacier where the family had always buried its secrets.

I had called it paranoia. I had called it grief. I had never once called it the truth.

The clock in the hall struck two. The wind dropped, suddenly, and in that silence the hotel seemed to hold its breath. I was drifting toward sleep when the scream came.

It was not a woman's scream, and it was not a cry of fear. It was a man's voice torn out of him, rising from the east wing in a single raw note that cut through the walls and the snow and the dark.

I was out of bed before the sound had died, running down the corridor with my heart slamming against my ribs. Behind me, in the dark, other doors opened, other feet began to run.

The scream had come from Arthur's suite. And when I reached the heavy oak door at the end of the hall, I found it locked from the inside.

chapters.name: The Locked Door
chapters.content:
Sheriff Calder arrived with a crowbar, which told me everything I needed to know about the kind of man he had become.

He had been a sergeant on the city force back when I was the detective they put in the papers. We had never liked each other. He believed order was a thing you enforced; I believed it was a thing you found out. Ten years and one scandal later, he had traded the city for a badge reading SHERIFF across a mountain county, and I had traded my badge for whoever paid. The mountain had shrunk us both, though in different directions.

He had come up that afternoon on county business, serving papers on Arthur, and the blizzard had stranded him like the rest of us. When the scream woke the hotel, he was the second man at my back, and he was not happy to find me there.

"You," he said. "Of all the rooms on this mountain."

The door to Arthur's suite was oak, four inches thick, hung in a frame as old as the hotel. The handle would not budge. Through a finger's gap in the frame I could see the head of a solid brass bolt seated deep in its keeper.

"Locked from the inside," I said.

"Then he's locked himself in," Calder said, "and he can bloody well unlock it. Pemberton! Arthur Pemberton!"

Silence. The wind had picked up again, and beyond it there was nothing but the weight of the hotel.

"He's not coming," I said.

"How do you know?"

"Because the scream came from in here," I said, "and no one has come out."

We put our shoulders to the door together. It was like pushing against a cliff. Elias the porter materialized out of the dark with the crowbar and a face that betrayed nothing, and between the three of us we worked the bar into the gap and heaved. The frame groaned; the bolt held. We heaved again, and somewhere deep in the oak something gave with a sound like a bone breaking, and the door sagged open.

The room was warm. That was the first thing I noticed, and it was wrong. The fire had burned low, but the air was close and hot, as if the room had been sealed tight for hours. The curtains were drawn across the tall windows. On the writing desk, a lamp still burned.

Arthur Pemberton lay on the hearthrug between the desk and the fireplace, on his back, one arm flung out, his eyes open and fixed on the ceiling. The front of his dressing gown was dark and wet, and the rug beneath him had drunk it up in a black bloom. There was blood on the marble of the hearth, and a smear where his hand had dragged.

I knelt. The wounds were in his chest — two of them, close together, driven deep and straight. A third mark, shallower, cut across the inside of his left forearm: a defensive gash, the kind a man makes when he throws up an arm to catch a blade coming for his heart.

"He's dead," I said. "Stabbed."

Calder stood over me, hands on his hips. "Stabbed himself. Man locks himself in, works himself up to it, puts the knife in and falls. Happens all the time. You'd know that if you'd ever kept a job in law enforcement long enough."

"Two wounds in the chest, Sheriff. No man stabs himself twice."

"People do strange things when they're desperate."

"And then cuts his own arm trying to stop himself?" I lifted Arthur's wrist, turned it to the lamplight. "That's a defensive wound. He threw his arm up. Against someone."

Behind me in the doorway the others had gathered — Marcus Webb in a dressing gown with a bottle in his fist, Celia in white, Ruth Keene with her hand over her mouth. Only Elias had not come closer. He stood in the corridor with the crowbar, watching me with those pale eyes, and I could not tell what he knew.

"Everyone out," I said. "This is a murder scene now. Nobody touches anything."

Calder laughed — a short, ugly sound. "Listen to you. Hale, the city threw you out because you put an innocent man in prison to close a case, and now you want to come into my county and run a crime scene?"

"The city threw me out," I said, "because I was right and they wanted me to be quiet. You know it, and I know it."

For a moment his jaw worked. Then he stepped back with his arms folded, the smile of a man who has decided to watch a fool drown rather than throw him a rope. "Fine. Play detective. The door was bolted from inside. The windows are sealed shut." He crossed to the tall windows and rapped the glass. "Painted shut a hundred years ago and never opened since. Frost on the inside of the pane. Nobody's come through that window since Queen Victoria."

He was right. I checked the sashes myself — each painted into its frame so thoroughly that seam and glass had become a single surface, layered in a century of coats. The frost inside had never been disturbed.

"And the chimney?" Calder said, mocking now. "Go on. Check."

I knelt at the hearth and put my head into the flue. It was a narrow Victorian stack, barely wider than my shoulders, and it narrowed further as it rose, sooted and black. A child could not have climbed it. No one had come down it, and no one had gone up.

"The door was bolted," Calder counted on his fingers. "The windows are sealed. The chimney's a joke. And you want me to believe somebody walked in, killed him, and walked out through the wallpaper."

I stood up slowly, brushing soot from my hands. The room was small. There was no closet that could hold a man — I opened the one door to a linen press and found it empty. The bed was undisturbed; beneath it, nothing but dust. The desk held paper, ink, and a cold cup of tea.

And no knife. I searched the room with the thoroughness of a man with nothing left to lose — under the cushions, behind the curtains, between the books on the shelf, in the cold grate, through his pockets, beneath the rug.

There was no weapon.

"Look at you," Calder said softly from the doorway. "Down on your hands and knees in a dead man's room. The great Victor Hale, undone by his own arrogance."

I got to my feet. My heart was still hammering, and behind my eyes a thought was circling that I did not yet want to name.

"He was stabbed twice," I said. "He fought back. The door was bolted from the inside, the windows were sealed, and there is no knife in this room. You tell me how that is suicide, Sheriff, and I'll write your statement myself."

Calder opened his mouth. Closed it. For the first time since he had come up the mountain, he had nothing to say.

Outside, the wind screamed across the peak. In the corridor, the stranded guests stood in their nightclothes like mourners at their own wake. And on the hearthrug at my feet, Arthur Pemberton lay staring at a ceiling he would never see, his murderer as gone as if he had never been.

The room was sealed. The body was murdered. And the killer had vanished into thin air.

chapters.name: The Suspects
chapters.content:
We moved the living into the great hall because none of us could bear the sight of the dead one. Calder threw wood on the fire, and the guests arranged themselves as at dinner, only the empty chair now wore a dead man's name. Murder changes a room. It deepens every shadow and makes people choose sides before they know they've chosen.

I stood with my back to the fire so I could watch them all at once. Calder settled into a wingback chair with his notepad and the look of a man watching a circus he'd paid to see fail. Elias lit every lamp in the hall with the patience of a man laying out a game he already knows how to win.

"Let's be sensible," Calder said. "There is no mystery here. The door was bolted from inside. The windows were sealed. The chimney's a pipe. Pemberton took his own life, and that's the long and short of it."

"Then where's the knife?" I asked.

"Fell down the chimney. Burned in the fire."

"Show me ash enough to account for a blade." I let him chew on that. "Two wounds in the chest, driven deep, and a defensive gash on the arm a man gives himself only when he's fighting for his life. He was killed by someone. And that someone is in this room."

Nobody looked at anybody. That was the trouble with a room full of people who all had reason not to.

"Mr. Webb. You were nearest to Arthur in business and in temper. Where were you when the scream came?"

Marcus Webb had set his bottle down at last, which I took as a bad sign — a drunk who stops drinking to think is a man suddenly afraid. He folded his arms and fixed me with a salesman's smile that didn't reach his eyes.

"In the lounge, Mr. Hale. Alone, with a decanter. Arthur had been locking himself in that suite for days, refusing to sign, running his own company into the ground out of spite. I heard the scream like everyone else."

"Anyone see you in the lounge?"

"Does a man need a witness to drink alone?" His jaw tightened. "It was empty. But I was the last man on earth Arthur would have opened that door for, and I couldn't have gotten through it if he had. Bolted from inside, wasn't it?"

It was. And that was the devil of it.

"Celia Pemberton." I turned to her. She sat composed in the deepest chair, a shawl around her shoulders, her face a mask polished by a lifetime of spotlights. "You were where?"

"In my room. With a headache." She said it the way actresses say lines they've grown tired of. "I took my tonic and lay in the dark. The scream woke me, and I came down to find my husband dead. I won't pretend I loved him, and I won't pretend I'm sorry."

Her hands lay folded in her lap, white and cold, pressed together as if to warm them. Cold hands, in a room with a roaring fire.

"Your tonic — laudanum, wasn't it?" I said. "Laudanum makes for a heavy sleep. Yet you woke at a scream through two wings of this hotel. Either your headache was a lie or your sleep was." "He threatened it, yes. But I didn't need to kill him. I only needed to outlive his moods, and I'd been doing that for years."

"Ruth." I softened my voice because she was trembling, and because I believed her grief, even if not her innocence. "You were typing, I'm told."

"In his study." Her voice was small and precise, the voice of a woman who had spent twenty years making herself useful and invisible. "He had left letters to be answered. I heard him cry out and I dropped everything and ran."

She clutched her purse to her chest, knuckles white around the clasp, and I watched her do it twice. A woman holding a purse like that is holding more than a handkerchief. "Please. I worked for him for twenty years. He was the only decent thing in my life."

"His will," I said gently. "You knew what was in it."

Her breath caught. "Everyone knew. He was always talking about it. The will, the will. As if it were the only thing that mattered." Her fingers tightened on the purse again. "But I never — I swear to you, on his memory, I never."

"Elias." I turned to the porter, who had finished with the lamps and stood with his back to the wall, patient as stone. "You were on your rounds. You heard it too."

"I heard it," Elias said. His voice was low and even, with the mountain in it. "But I saw something first."

The hall went quiet. Even Calder leaned forward.

"Before the scream," Elias went on, "I was coming up the east-wing stairs with the lamp. There's a band of light beneath Mr. Pemberton's door. And I saw a shadow pass across that light. Someone moving inside his room, from the desk toward the fireplace."

"Could it have been Arthur himself? A man moving about his own room casts a shadow under his own door."

Elias shook his head slowly. "Then he cried out. I heard him plain, through the wood. He said — and this I will swear on the book — he said, 'You're dead.' Not a question. Not a shout of fear. 'You're dead.' And then the scream."

"'You're dead.'" I repeated it, and the words hung in the warm air like frost. "As if he'd seen someone he knew to be dead. As if he were speaking to a ghost."

"He was," Ruth whispered, and pressed her hand over her mouth as if she'd said too much.

The fire popped. Outside, the wind flung snow against the glass, and for a long moment no one spoke. Four faces in the lamplight, each with a lie half-built behind its eyes: Marcus with his ruin and his hatred, Celia with her cold hands, Ruth with her purse and her ghost, and Elias, who saw shadows under doors and spoke of the dead as if they walked.

Calder slapped his notebook shut. "This is nonsense. A shadow and a cry, and you want to hang somebody on it? The door was bolted from the inside, with a brass bolt I saw with my own eyes. Nobody came out of that room. Nobody could have. If it wasn't suicide, the killer is still in there — and I searched it myself. There's no one in there but a dead man."

"The killer isn't in the room, Sheriff. The killer was in the room. There's a difference."

"Then where is he now? The snow's six feet deep in the pass. Nobody's gone anywhere tonight."

"Then he's still in this hotel." I let my eyes move across them, one by one. "In this hall. Standing in this firelight, listening to us argue about how impossible he is."

Nobody moved. Outside, the blizzard screamed across the peak, sealing us in together, murderer and all.

"The room was sealed," I said, "and yet Arthur Pemberton is dead by another hand. One of you knows how. Before this storm breaks, I'm going to find out which."

Calder laughed, but it was a thin, nervous sound that died quickly in the empty spaces of the hall.

It was well past three in the morning, and the killer was among us. Arthur's telegram had said the answer was in the wall. I meant to find out if he'd been telling the truth.

chapters.name: The Letter
chapters.content:
The great hall was settling into that exhausted, quarrelsome silence that follows a murder when nobody is allowed to leave. I left them to it. Calder had his notebook and his certainty, and the guests had their alibis and their secrets, and none of it was doing me any good. The answer, if there was one, was not in their faces. Arthur had told me where to find it, and I had spent the night too busy listening to living liars to hear the dead man.

I took the east-wing stairs alone. Elias had left a lamp burning at the turn, and the corridor beyond was a tunnel of old wallpaper and colder air. The door to Arthur's suite stood ajar, gaping where we had broken it. I went in and shut it behind me as well as it would shut.

The room was exactly as we had left it, which is to say, exactly as Arthur had died in it. The fire had sunk to a bed of dull coals. The lamp on the writing desk still burned, throwing the same long shadows. And on the hearthrug between desk and fireplace lay Arthur Pemberton, on his back, his eyes fixed on the ceiling, the blood dried black on his dressing gown.

I knelt beside him first, because I owed him that. Then I got to work.

I went through the room the way I had gone through it once with Calder watching and laughing — but slower now, with my hands instead of my pride. Under the cushions again. Between the books. Behind the curtains. On the back of the writing chair hung Arthur's coat — not the dressing gown he had died in, but the dark wool coat he had been wearing when he shut himself in here days ago. It looked like a thing left for the morning, as if he had expected to walk out of that room alive. I nearly passed it by. Then I thought of the telegram, folded in my own breast pocket, and I put my hand inside the coat instead.

The inner pocket gave up a letter. Cream paper, creased along old folds, addressed in Arthur's hand: To Victor Hale, in the event of my death.

My name in his writing. The room went very quiet.

The letter was dated that very day — hours before the scream.

"Victor — you came. I knew you would come, though I gave you every reason not to. You think me a madman for the letters. Perhaps I am. But I am not mad about this. My brother Silas is alive. I have seen him. He is here, in this house, hiding in the old places, waiting. He knows the old ways of this house — passages no one remembers, doors no one sees. Twenty years I thought him drowned, and twenty years he has been biding his time in my shadow. He means to take back what was taken from him. If I am found dead, the answer is in the wall. Forgive me. Forgive me for everything. — Arthur"

The words blurred. I had read his earlier letters with a pitying smile, skimmed them over coffee, filed them under paranoia. "He is alive," Arthur had written, again and again, and I had told myself the man was cracked, that grief and guilt over the drowning had curdled into obsession. I had taken his money because money was real, and set his terror aside because terror was not. And now he was dead, and his coat pocket had proved him saner than I had ever been.

Guilt sat down on my chest like a stone. I read the letter twice more, then folded it into my own pocket, next to the telegram, where the two warnings could keep each other company.

Then I did the thing I should have done the first time, with my eyes and not my temper. I re-tested the locked room.

The door first. The frame had split around the keeper when we forced it, and the brass bolt still stood in its seat, thrown deep from the inside — no keyhole, no gap wide enough for a hand, and the keeper bright where the bolt had worn it. Whoever had shot that bolt had done it from within, and then stayed.

The windows next. A century of paint had welded the sashes into their frames; the frost lay undisturbed on the inner glass, and not a latch had moved since the room was last sealed. The chimney last, narrow as a pipe, sooted black, closing to nothing above the grate. A child could not have climbed it.

Three exits. All sealed. All sealed from within.

The letter said the answer was in the wall. I had spent the whole night believing the walls were honest, because I had measured them and found them solid. I had tapped nothing. I had searched the room for a weapon and a killer, and never once for a door.

I began with my knuckles on the fireplace surround — the oak panels that ran from the hearth to the ceiling. Solid. I worked along the chimney breast. Solid. I moved to the wainscoting beside the desk, rapping panel by panel, listening the way a man listens to a heartbeat.

And there, where the wainscoting met the chimney breast, behind a heavy oak panel that the lamplight had always made look like every other panel, the wood answered differently. Not the dead thud of oak against stone. A hollow sound. The sound of a space where no space should be.

I dropped to my knees and looked. The seam was nearly invisible — a hairline in the grain, so fine that a lifetime of eyes had passed it over. But it was there, and where a man's thumb might rest there was a faint polish in the varnish, worn by years of use and decades of forgetting.

My hands were shaking. I got out my penknife and worked the blade into the seam. The oak resisted, then gave with a dry groan, and the panel swung toward me on hidden hinges.

Cold air breathed out of the wall, carrying dust and something older — the smell of disuse, of stone and rust and faint, stale tobacco. I held the lamp up.

Beyond the panel was a narrow dark opening, just wide enough for a man's shoulders, going down into blackness. The old ways of the house. Arthur's words, in his own hand.

The answer was in the wall. And Arthur had left me the key.

chapters.name: The Priest-Hole
chapters.content:
The opening was narrow, shoulder-wide, and it went down. I knelt in the cold air that breathed out of the wall, held the lamp into the dark, and for a long moment I did not move, because what I was looking at was impossible and I needed to be sure.

It was a priest-hole — one of those hidden compartments built into the thickness of an old wall, tall enough for a man to stand in, just wide enough to breathe in, a place to be forgotten alive. This one was roughly six feet of vertical blackness, its floor a foot below the level of the room, its far wall the raw brick of the old chimney core.

I swung my legs over the sill and lowered myself in. Dust puffed up in a gray cloud, thick enough to taste. When it settled I played the lamp across the floor, and my heart went cold.

The dust was disturbed. Not by age and not by mice. There were footprints in it — fresh, clear, the toe prints deep where a man had climbed in and out. A man had stood in this hole, in the dark, and waited.

And beside the nearer footprint lay a cufflink.

I crouched and picked it up. Gold, black enamel, still warm-tinged from the body that had worn it. On the back, scratched deep, two initials. S.P.

Silas Pemberton.

I turned it over in my fingers, and the sealed room above rearranged itself in my head like a picture falling into place. Arthur had not been mad. He had written the truth in his own hand, and the truth had been standing in this hole when Arthur threw the bolt, and had climbed out after the scream, and the door had been locked from the inside the whole time because the man had never needed the door at all.

Then I looked at the back wall, and the picture fell apart.

I ran my palm over the brick. Solid. I tapped it — the flat, honest sound of brick against mortar, no give anywhere. I worked my penknife into the joints. The mortar crumbled at the touch, but behind it was brick, and behind the brick, when I put my ear to the cold surface, the muffled silence of solid mass. I went over every inch of that compartment, and the answer was the same as it had been all night: no exit.

A hiding place, yes. A way out, no.

So the impossible simply shifted its shape. The killer had hidden here — the footprints said so, the cufflink said so, the stale tobacco said so. But he had hidden here with the room sealed, and the room was still sealed, and I could find no way for him to leave it. A man could climb into the priest-hole from the room above. What I could not find was any way for that man to leave it at all.

Unless he was still in it.

The thought sat cold in my chest. I stood up in the narrow dark, turned a slow circle with the lamp held high, and saw nothing but brick, dust, and my own shadow.

I pocketed the cufflink. It was the only thing of weight the place had given me, and I took it like a man taking the one coin from a dead man's purse.

"A dead end," I said aloud, to hear a voice in the dark. "A hiding place and a dead end."

I was halfway out, my elbows on the sill, when a voice said, "Mr. Hale?"

I nearly dropped the lamp.

Ruth Keene stood in the doorway of the suite, one hand on the splintered frame, her face pale in the lamplight, her purse clutched to her chest like a shield.

"Miss Keene," I said, climbing out of the opening and brushing the dust from my knees. "You should be downstairs."

"I couldn't sleep." Her eyes went past me, to the open panel, to the blackness beyond it, and something in her face — I would have called it fear, except that fear had no business looking that specific. "I came to look for Arthur's will. He kept his papers in the study, but I thought... I thought perhaps he'd brought it in here. He was so afraid, these last days."

"You knew your way up here."

"I knew the way to everything Arthur kept." She said it simply, without pride. Then: "What is that?"

I could have lied. Instead I watched her face and told her the truth. "A priest-hole," I said. "Hidden in the wall. Someone has been standing in it recently. Fresh boots, and a taste for tobacco."

The color drained out of her. She took one step back, then stopped herself, and her hands tightened around her purse until the knuckles went white. For a second I thought she would speak. Then she shook her head, a small, quick movement, as if refusing the words before they reached her lips.

"I have to go," she said, already backing into the corridor. "You shouldn't have opened that, Mr. Hale. Whatever it is — you shouldn't have opened it."

Her heels clicked away down the east-wing corridor, and I let her go. I had learned long ago that a frightened witness will tell you everything, given enough rope. And Ruth Keene had just told me more than she knew: she had not asked what I found in the hole. She had asked what the hole was. A woman looking for a will does not care about the architecture.

I turned back to the priest-hole, and that was when I saw it.

The lamp, still held low, caught the back wall at an angle, and in that glancing light the line of the brick was too regular. Not the staggered, careless pattern of old bricklaying, every course a little off. This line ran straight as a ruled edge across the middle of the wall — too straight, too even, the way a line runs when a man has drawn it on purpose and then built over it to hide what he drew.

A door, I thought. A door in the brick.

I stepped toward the opening, my blood loud in my ears, and put my hand on the frame —

And somewhere in the house, a woman screamed.

It came from the other end of the corridor, thin and sharp through the walls, a scream of pure animal fright. I knew that sound. I had heard it at the other end of this same night, and I had found a dead man at the end of it.

I let go of the frame, blew out the lamp, and ran.

chapters.name: The Shadow Under the Door
chapters.content:
The scream died the way screams die when the throat that made them gives out. I ran toward it, past Arthur's door, past the turn where the wallpaper blistered with damp, and found Celia Pemberton at the far end of the east wing, pressed flat against the wall, her hand at her mouth.

She wore a robe over her nightgown, her hair loose, her bare feet blue on the boards.

"What happened?" I said.

"There." She pointed at the skirting, where a gap was gnawed through into the wall. "A rat. It ran over my foot. God, I thought — I thought it was him."

"Him?"

"Arthur. I heard footsteps. I came out to see who was walking, and something ran across my foot, and I screamed like a fool." She laughed, a thin, practised sound that fooled no one. "An actress's instincts. Scream first, think later."

The gap was real enough. Rat droppings lay in the dust beside it, the wood gnawed smooth with age. It was exactly the kind of thing that makes a woman scream at four in the morning in a house with a corpse in it. That was the trouble. It was too exactly that.

"Your hands are cold," I said.

"Of course they are. It's freezing."

"They were cold this afternoon too, in a room with a roaring fire." I watched her face. "You said your tonic knocked you flat. Yet you hear footsteps through two wings of this house and come out in your bare feet to investigate."

Her chin went up. The actress gathered the robe, found the line. "I don't know what you're implying, Mr. Hale, and I don't care to. My husband is dead, and I am a widow, and I will not be picked apart by a disgraced policeman with a grudge against the world."

She walked back toward the stairs, and I let her go. I did not believe in her rat. I believed Celia Pemberton had wanted to know what I had found in the wall, and had screamed to pull me out of that suite before I found it.

Which meant I had to go back. But first, there was a man in the great hall who had seen a shadow under a door, and I had let his testimony sit long enough.

Elias was where I had left him, against the wall with his arms folded, watching the fire as if the flames were telling him something. The others had drifted into exhausted sleep — Marcus snoring in a chair, Ruth curled in a corner with her purse clutched to her chest. Only Calder looked up when I came in, and only Elias met my eyes.

"Again," I said. "Start at the beginning, and leave nothing out."

Elias did not argue. He had the patience of a man who knows his story will be believed eventually.

"I was coming up the east-wing stairs with the lamp," he said. "A little before two. The house was quiet. Mr. Pemberton had been locked in his suite for days — I brought his meals, and he took them at the door, never showing his face. That night there was a band of light under his door. He always kept the lamp burning. He was afraid of the dark, Mr. Hale. A grown man, afraid of the dark."

"Go on."

"I saw the shadow pass across the light. Slow, like a man crossing the room. From the desk toward the fireplace. I stopped on the landing, because it wasn't Mr. Pemberton's walk — I'd watched his shadow under that door for a week, and I knew it. This was someone else's."

"And then?"

"Then I heard him, through the wood, plain as I'm speaking now. He said, 'You're dead.' And then he screamed — not shouted, screamed — and there was the sound of something falling, the crash of a chair, and I ran for the sheriff."

Calder grunted. "A man alone can say 'You're dead' to himself. Men talk to themselves when they're frightened. I've heard it a hundred times."

"To himself?" I said. "Then who threw the bolt, Sheriff?"

"The bolt was thrown from inside. We know that."

"We know the bolt was thrown from inside," I said slowly, "and we know the room was lit. In a lit room, a shadow under the door is made by a body moving between the lamp and the door. A man alone could make such a shadow. He could even cry out to a ghost he believed in. But a man alone cannot be stabbed twice in the chest, slash his own arm defending himself, and hide the knife where no knife is. One impossibility I can forgive. Three I cannot."

I stood over the fire, letting the shape of it settle, and when I spoke again it was to Elias, because he was the only one who had been there.

"You say the shadow moved from the desk toward the fireplace. The band of light is under the door. For you to see it at all, the man who made it had to be between the lamp and the door — crossing the room, toward the hearth. Arthur cried out at him. Not at a ghost. At someone he knew was dead, standing in his room with the bolt thrown and the door locked. And that man was still in the room when Arthur screamed."

Calder's notepad went still. "That's impossible. I searched that room to the rafters. There's no one in it but a corpse."

"Not when you searched it. But when Arthur screamed — yes." I turned for the stairs. "The killer was in the room when the bolt was thrown. He had to be. He was there before Arthur locked himself in, and he hid where a man could hide while you and I tore the room apart. He hid in the wall."

"The priest-hole," Ruth whispered from her corner, and I saw her eyes go wide as she realized she had said it aloud.

I did not stop to answer her. I took the east-wing stairs two at a time, past the rat's gap in the skirting, to the splintered door of Arthur's suite. The panel still stood open in the wainscoting, and the cold air still breathed out of the dark.

I had looked at the brick wall of that hole and called it a dead end. But a man who has hidden in a space the size of a coffin, waiting for his dead brother's twin to throw a bolt, does not need a dead end. He needs a way out.

And the line of that brick had been too straight, too even — like a line a man draws on purpose before he builds over it.

I knelt, struck a match, and went down into the dark after the truth.

chapters.name: The Forged Signature
chapters.content:
The brick gave nothing. I knelt in the dark of the priest-hole, lamp held low, and ran my fingers along the too-straight line where the courses refused to stagger. I could feel the door behind it the way you feel a man's presence through a wall. My penknife found the joint and bit. Behind the mortar, brick; and behind the brick, when I pressed my ear to the cold, the muffled, breathing silence of space. Not mass. Space.

And in the dust at my knees, where a body had braced itself to work a mechanism, a black smear of grease, thumb-wide, still tacky.

That was when I heard it — the soft crackle of paper feeding a fire, and with it the smell of burning. Not coal. Not the pine of the house fires. Paper, ink, and the bitter sharpness of hot wax.

I was out of the hole in seconds, through the suite, down the east wing. The study door stood open. Ruth Keene crouched at the hearth, feeding a document to the flames sheet by sheet, her face lit orange, her purse gaping on the desk like a mouth.

"Miss Keene."

She spun. The half-burned page fluttered toward the fire, and I crossed the room and snatched it out of the grate before the last corner caught. I beat out the flame with my bare hand, swore, and held the remains to the light.

It was a power of attorney. I had seen a hundred of them in my insurance years. This one transferred all of Arthur Pemberton's assets — his holdings, his company, the hotel itself — into the keeping of Ruth Keene, to be held and disposed of at her discretion. Dated three days before his death.

And the signature was Arthur's name, written in the shaking, careful hand of a child copying a lesson. I had Arthur's true hand in the letter in my pocket. This was a tracing, and a clumsy one, the letters wavering where the pencil had slipped, the ink gone thick where the pen had hovered.

"Forged," I said.

She did not argue. She sat back on her heels and began to cry, the way people cry when a thing carried too long finally breaks them. "Yes," she whispered. "Yes, it's forged. I traced it from an old contract. I know what it looks like."

"Why?"

"To protect him." She wiped her face with the back of her hand. "Marcus Webb has been stealing from Arthur for a year. Siphoning the company dry, and the hotel with it. Arthur wouldn't see it. He trusted Marcus. When I tried to tell him, he said I was a jealous old woman who didn't understand business."

"So you forged this."

"So I could take everything out of Marcus's reach before he took the last of it." She looked up, her face naked in a way I had not seen on any face in this house. "Arthur was dying of worry. He kept the lamp burning because the dark brought him visions. I would have forged a hundred signatures to buy him one more week of peace."

"Miss Keene." I crouched in front of her. "Three days ago. Did you see Marcus go into Arthur's room?"

Her breath caught. "Yes," she said. "The night before Arthur locked himself in. I was coming up the back stairs and I saw him come out of Arthur's door, very late, buttoning his coat. I never told anyone. I was afraid of what it meant."

"Come downstairs," I said. "We'll ask him what it meant."

Marcus Webb was awake when we came into the great hall. I laid the charred document on the table before him and told him what Ruth had said.

He stared at the paper as if it were a snake. "She's lying. She's been lying since the day she set foot in that office. Arthur's assets — she wanted them for herself. That's why she forged it."

"You were in his room," I said. "The night before he locked himself in. She saw you come out."

"I never—" Marcus began, and Celia's voice cut across him from the stairs, cold and precise, the voice of a woman who has waited a long time for her line.

"Of course he was in Arthur's room, Mr. Hale. Marcus and Ruth were lovers. For years, while I was married to that man, they met in the east wing." She descended into the light. "Ask her about the purse she clutches like a rosary. She keeps his letters in it."

Ruth had gone the color of paper. "That was years ago. And it ended when I saw what Marcus was doing to Arthur's company. It ended the night I found the thefts."

"Convenient," Celia said.

I looked at the four of them — the drunk, the actress, the secretary with her secrets, the porter watching the flames — and the locked room made less sense than ever. Marcus wanted Arthur dead and the company with him. Celia wanted her inheritance. Ruth wanted to protect a man who had trusted her, and she had forged his name, and she had stood inside the priest-hole. Every one of them had a motive. None of them had a way past a bolted door.

Ruth gathered her purse and stood. "I've told you the truth. All of it. I'm going to my room."

She turned to go, and as she passed me the firelight caught her sleeve — a long, dark smear of grease, black and shiny, running from her elbow to her wrist. The same grease I had knelt in at the bottom of the priest-hole, where the mechanism of the false brick had left its black thumbprint in the dust.

The same grease. On Ruth Keene's arm.

She had been inside the compartment. Not a visitor come to look — a woman who had climbed in and out, who had worked the hidden door, who had stood in that coffin of brick and dust in the dark.

Her purse. I understood it now. She had clutched it all night like a shield because it held the forgery she was burning sheet by sheet. What mattered was that she had known the way in.

I did not stop her. I let her go, and when her footsteps had faded I was already moving, taking the east-wing stairs two at a time, back to Arthur's suite, back to the open panel and the too-straight line of brick.

The priest-hole was not a dead end. Ruth Keene had proved that with her sleeve.

I struck a match and went down into the dark.
